title: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904–1905
author: Christopher Martin
verdict: A good first book: it provides a chronology on which to place memoirs and specialist studies.
annotation: A British historian looks at the war from outside, taking neither Russia’s nor Japan’s side, and calmly examines why Russia lost a war it had assumed it would win. The book follows the main events without drowning in detail, then carries the story to 1945 to show how the outcome shaped the Far East for forty years. Its weakness is its age: Martin worked with what a Western author could access in the 1960s, and some of his judgments have since been revised. Read them as opinions rather than final verdicts.

title: In the Russo-Japanese War
author: Vikenty Veresayev
verdict: If you read one literary eyewitness account of this war, make it this one: a sobering corrective to tales of heroes.
annotation: The notes of a military doctor who travelled with a field hospital through Manchuria, Mukden and the retreat, then returned home along a Trans-Siberian Railway gripped by revolution. The main enemies are behind the lines: offices, supply officials and reports that matter more than people. His voice is calm, like a doctor making a diagnosis; the retreat after Mukden produces the strongest pages. Contemporaries accused him of being unpatriotic, but today the book conveys pain more than mockery, and its scenes of bureaucratic reporting need little explanation. Chapters appeared soon after the war; the complete book was published in 1928.

title: Russian Port Arthur in 1904: A History of Everyday Military Life
author: Alexander Lysev
verdict: After this book, Port Arthur becomes more than a line in a textbook: people baked bread and grew cucumbers under shellfire.
annotation: Instead of assaults and disputes over who surrendered the fortress, Lysev asks how people lived in besieged Port Arthur: what soldiers, sailors, officers and civilians ate, where they slept and what they did between bombardments. He draws on 83 files from 12 collections in the Russian State Naval Archive and Russian State Historical Archive: ration returns and records of bathhouses, bakeries, water supplies, food smuggling and military vegetable plots. Alongside them are Kolchak’s notebook, Rimsky-Korsakov’s diary and the recollections of midshipmen and sailors, allowing official records and personal accounts to check each other. It reads like reportage: sit down for a moment and two hours disappear.

title: Diary of the Siege of Port Arthur
author: Mikhail Lilje
verdict: An account by a participant in the siege, best read with a pencil in hand.
annotation: An army engineer captain first built Kwantung’s defences, then spent eleven months defending them, keeping a diary from January 1904 to January 1905. His prose is literary; his engineer’s eye precise and sometimes merciless: the squadron’s unreadiness on the first night, the loss of Petropavlovsk, scurvy, quarrels among commanders, the “Calvary of Arthur” on 203 Metre Hill and the dejected garrison on surrender day. Lilje was a witness, not a historian: he saw his own sector and heard staff rumours, so his harsh judgments of the commanders need checking against other sources. The diary was not published until 2002.

title: Light and Shadows of the Russo-Japanese War, 1904–5: Letters to My Wife
author: Yevgeny Botkin
verdict: One of the war’s most humane testimonies: few grand strategies, plenty of hardship and compassion.
annotation: Letters to his wife from a doctor who volunteered for Manchuria and headed the Red Cross medical service with the army in the field. In 1918 he would die with the imperial family in the Ipatiev House. He wrote warmly, sometimes with humour, trying to dwell on the “light”; the “shadows” stand out when they break through: shrapnel at Wafangou, now Wafangdian, part of Dalian, and typhus and dysentery that killed doctors and nurses. Readers living in China may especially enjoy his observations of counting and etiquette, houses, theatre and the Mukden tombs.

title: Kondratenko: Hero of the Defence of Port Arthur
author: Sergei Kulichkin
verdict: A colonel writes about a general with few awkward questions and such affection that halfway through you begin to admire the hero with him.
annotation: A volume in the Lives of Remarkable People series by a professional soldier who had already written the novella In Port Arthur. Kondratenko is an engineer, strategist, father to his soldiers and apparently the only adult in the besieged city; as in Stepanov, Stessel takes the blame for surrender. The book faithfully continues the Soviet tradition in which a tsarist general becomes the model commander, only in different epaulettes. Expect few new facts; its interest lies in the tone and details: his Tiflis origins, strong wine rather than vodka and the clear head of the defence commander.

title: A Reformer after the Reforms: S. Yu. Witte and Russian Society, 1906–1915
author: Ella Saginadze
verdict: How the retired Witte managed to irritate everyone and became a character in newspapers, drawing rooms and on stage.
annotation: Saginadze examines how newspapers, drawing rooms, satirists and the theatre saw Witte after his retirement in 1906. The right called him an “enemy of the Russian people”; Lenin, a “clown minister”. The empress blamed him for the October Manifesto, the liberals for its failure to become a constitution. Every contemporary anxiety attached itself to the count: the stock exchange, foreign capital, Jews, Germans and suspicions that he wanted to become “president”. The reverse is visible too: Witte cultivated the press as perhaps Russia’s first public politician. This book underpins the channel’s concluding post on him.

title: Memoirs
author: Sergei Witte
verdict: The era’s best collection of compromising stories, allowing for the fact that Witte is always right in his own memoirs.
annotation: Three volumes written and revised after Witte’s retirement, with the manuscripts kept in a French bank beyond the police’s reach. His widow took them abroad, and they appeared in Berlin in the early 1920s, edited by Iosif Hessen. They are indispensable: much of the era is still seen through Witte’s eyes. But this is testimony from an interested party. Historians Ananyich and Ganelin showed how often he settled scores and reshaped the past in his own favour. Here too, relayed through Kuropatkin, appears Plehve’s supposed remark about a “small victorious war”, whose authenticity is very doubtful.

title: Sergei Yulyevich Witte and His Times
author: Boris Ananyich, Rafail Ganelin
verdict: The best scholarly biography of Witte in Russian: a good place to begin.
annotation: This book heads the further-reading list accompanying the posts on Witte. Its authors are leading specialists in the empire’s financial and political history, and the historians who demonstrated the bias in Witte’s memoirs and his habit of rewriting the past to his advantage. A useful counterweight to the Memoirs: it helps distinguish the minister as he was from the figure he wished posterity to remember.

title: Witte
author: S. V. Ilyin
verdict: A popular biography in the Lives of Remarkable People series, lighter than the academic studies.
annotation: A biography of Witte published by Molodaya Gvardiya in the Lives of Remarkable People series. The channel recommends it as a more accessible alternative to Ananyich and Ganelin’s scholarly biography. For readers who want a continuous account of his life after the posts on “Count Half-Sakhalin”, without a full scholarly apparatus.

title: Russia and International Capital, 1897–1914
author: Boris Ananyich
verdict: Loans, the gold ruble and dependence on French money: a good companion to Molodyakov.
annotation: A study of the money behind Witte’s empire: foreign loans, the gold ruble and growing dependence on French capital. The channel recommends it alongside Molodyakov’s book on the Franco-Russian alliance. Where that explains why St Petersburg and Paris drew together, this shows what the alliance cost in rubles and francs. It matters to Dalny and Port Arthur because French money reached the Chinese Eastern Railway and Kwantung through the Russo-Chinese Bank.

title: S. Yu. Witte: Financier, Politician, Diplomat
author: A. P. Korelin, S. A. Stepanov
verdict: On the channel’s short list for readers who want to learn more about Witte.
annotation: A book from the further-reading list accompanying the Witte series. Its title names three sides of his career: finance, politics and diplomacy. The channel covers the same subjects through the gold ruble, the October Manifesto, the agreement with Li Hongzhang and the Treaty of Portsmouth. The channel’s author has not offered a separate assessment of this book.

title: S. Yu. Witte as a Diplomat
author: A. V. Ignatyev
verdict: On the channel’s short list for readers chiefly interested in Witte’s diplomacy.
annotation: A further-reading recommendation on Witte’s foreign policy. For the channel’s readers, its relevance is above all the Far East: the treaty with Li Hongzhang, the Chinese Eastern Railway, the Kwantung lease and the Portsmouth negotiations that earned Witte the nickname “Count Half-Sakhalin”. The channel’s author has not offered a separate assessment.

title: Russia and France: An Entente Cordiale, 1889–1900
author: Vasily Molodyakov
verdict: A useful companion: it shows how French money reached Port Arthur, and the title seems deliberately ambiguous.
annotation: A historian of Japan and French nationalism traces the brief “golden age” of an alliance between autocratic empire and republic: Alexander III standing bareheaded for the Marseillaise at Kronstadt, Russian sailors in Toulon. Behind the romance lay calculation: France needed an ally against Germany, Russia needed money. For Dalny, the connection was direct: French capital established the Russo-Chinese Bank, which financed the Chinese Eastern Railway, and France joined Russia in forcing Japan to return Liaodong. The irony is that Paris remained neutral in 1904 and signed its own entente cordiale with London.

title: Liaodong and Its Ports: Port Arthur and Dalianwan
author: Władysław Kotwicz, Leonid Borodovsky
verdict: Light reading with some curious details, and useful practice in pre-revolutionary Russian spelling.
annotation: A 47-page booklet published by Orientalists in summer 1898, five months after the Kwantung lease, as an inexpensive alternative to the Finance Ministry’s costly Description of Manchuria. It describes the bay where Dalny would be founded a year later: ruined forts, one pier, a street five paces wide, Shin-tai’s bakery and living costs a third of Vladivostok’s, “but no amusements whatsoever”. The authors argued for “Guan-dong” instead of “Kwantung” and lost; their prediction that Dalianwan would become northern China’s equivalent of Shanghai and Hong Kong proved sound. Available in the National Electronic Library.

title: Letters to My Neighbours, 1902–1904
author: Mikhail Menshikov
verdict: The elaborate prose takes effort, but century-old questions sound familiar.
annotation: Columns by a leading journalist of the early twentieth century, a former naval navigator who wrote for Suvorin’s Novoye Vremya on finance, drinking, schools, Tolstoy, Chekhov and the war with Japan. The central wartime essay is “Internal Defence” from 1904. Instead of analysing manoeuvres at Liaoyang, Menshikov asks about the condition of the country fighting the war, arguing that defeats in Manchuria begin in offices, schools and taverns. His sermon-like newspaper prose demands patience, but rewards it.

title: Anecdotes of the Russian Empire: The Russo-Japanese War
author: A. V. Shevchenko
verdict: An unlikely success: the commentary makes jokes from 1905 funny again.
annotation: Wartime jokes about Stessel, who has “already surrendered”, the fleet, which is “in Japan”, and the turmoil left after Portsmouth. A footnote usually kills a joke, but here the commentary is so well judged that the joke begins to work: once you know who Stessel was and what was signed at Portsmouth, you can laugh with the morning-paper readers. Such texts show whom society distrusted and what it understood before official bulletins caught up.

title: Cruisers
author: Valentin Pikul
verdict: A novel that can keep you awake until morning, with the proviso that you need a reference book to tell where Yegoryev ends and Pikul begins.
annotation: The Vladivostok Cruiser Detachment seen through the fictional midshipman Panafidin: Bogatyr, Rurik, the battle with Kamimura’s squadron, a cruiser’s sinking, captivity and return to a shattered fleet. The real Trusov, Jessen, Bezobrazov and Kamimura appear alongside him, with Yegoryev’s 1939 study providing the foundation. Short, sharp sentences and fast scenes keep you reading until two in the morning. Historians’ objections are fair: the invented hero sinks with the real Rurik, the romance and staff rival are fabricated, and the ending tends towards nineteenth-century sentimentality. But afterwards you will stop confusing Rurik with Varyag.

title: Port Arthur
author: Alexander Stepanov
verdict: Outdated as history, exemplary as a monument to Soviet fiction of the 1940s; read it to understand your grandfather’s firm views on Stessel.
annotation: A Stalin Prize in 1946 and millions of copies: a volume of Port Arthur can be found in almost every Russian country house. It is a model novel of its era, with roles assigned in advance: generals sell out, soldiers fight to the death. Stessel and Fok betray the fortress for five million, though the court said nothing about a sale; Kondratenko is canonised, Kolchak serves on the wrong ship and the romance is crushingly heavy. The author’s own story is another matter: archival research published in 2010 found that neither he nor his father had been inside the besieged fortress. His actual wartime life was harsher than the legend.

title: The Zvonaryov Family
author: Alexander Stepanov
verdict: The sequel to Port Arthur, where the “real horror” is only beginning.
annotation: An unfinished sequel to Port Arthur, written in 1959–1963 and covering 1905–1916. Its opening chapters overflow with strikes, labour unrest and Bolshevism; politics fills every line. The love triangle survives: on the First World War front, Zvonaryov, by then the father of three daughters, meets Nadya again and is “overwhelmed” by feeling. The channel’s author read both novels and considers that a very brave act.

title: The Crisis of Moral Consciousness in Russia and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905
author: A. L. Panishchev
verdict: Read it if you want an argument: “moral consciousness” here takes the place of shells rather than following them.
annotation: The study begins with the premise that souls, rather than battleships, lost the war and fits the whole story to that claim. The war itself arrives only around page 50, after Alexander II’s reforms and a “crisis of messianism”; there are more mirrors in the chapter titles than at Versailles. Moral decline cannot be measured but can explain anything, so Shimose explosive, the single-track Trans-Siberian and Kuropatkin’s decisions recede. Port Arthur’s defence gets about ten pages, Japanese culture three. An important subject becomes a sermon illustrated with history.

title: The Russo-Japanese War and the Bolsheviks’ Attitude towards It
author: Yemelyan Yaroslavsky
verdict: Little use for the war itself; revealing about how the USSR rewrote it.
annotation: A 48-page booklet from the 1930s by a party historian and the country’s leading atheist. Its thesis is blunt: tsarism’s defeat “revolutionised the masses”, the Bolsheviks “favoured defeat”, and Port Arthur, Mukden and Tsushima made a useful prelude to 1905. Lenin, Stalin and proclamations supply the evidence. The irony lies in its afterlife: in 1945 Stalin would call the same defeat a “black stain” the country had waited forty years to erase. Read the booklet beside that speech to see one event’s meaning reversed. The 2020 reprint’s cover, with Stalin above a map of Asia, already indicates the approach.

title: Ensigns of the Admiralty
author: Vladimir Poselyagin
verdict: A promise to rewrite the Russo-Japanese War produces boredom: it barely merits a facepalm.
annotation: The first volume of The Twins trilogy. A modern person’s mind inhabits twin brothers who become universal soldiers before finishing naval school, murder British bankers to block Japanese loans and sink destroyers by the dozen at Port Arthur to Makarov’s fatherly praise. Stessel naturally betrays the fortress for money, villains come labelled, every twist is visible three chapters ahead and there is no ending. The prose sounds like a favourite dream retold in a garage, full of “anyway” and “so we got them”, with antisemitic motifs besides. The channel’s conclusion: reread the real history; its plot is better.

title: Lieutenants of the Admiralty
author: Vladimir Poselyagin
verdict: Finished at 2.5× speed, and still a waste of time.
annotation: The second part of The Twins. Vitgeft brings the squadron safely to Vladivostok and becomes naval minister; in reality, a shell hit on Tsesarevich left only part of his leg. Russia and Japan settle for a draw. The brothers then learn night vision and telekinesis, fight in every war on earth for ten years, avenge themselves on journalists and single-handedly replace the fleet in the First World War. Knowing the future, they try to prevent nothing: they simply grow rich and shoot. No building, no doubts, just resentment and endless gunfire. Again, no ending.

title: On the Road to Collapse: The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905. A Military and Political History
author: Oleg Airapetov
verdict: The channel’s author recommends this as one of the best books in Russian for understanding the war as a whole.
annotation: A military and political history from Russia’s advance into the Far East to the army’s return after the Treaty of Portsmouth. Port Arthur is placed alongside diplomacy, finance and decisions in St Petersburg. Conclusions draw on documents, memoirs and correspondence. Moscow: Algoritm, 2014. 496 pp. Historical Discoveries series.

title: Russia and Japan: The Golden Age, 1905–1916
author: Vasily Molodyakov
verdict: Read after the books on the war; the reviewer questions the author’s “golden age” label.
annotation: The rapprochement of former enemies after Portsmouth: the conventions of 1907, 1910 and 1912, spheres of influence in Manchuria, arms deliveries and the 1916 treaty. The review draws attention to the cost of this friendship for China, Korea and Mongolia. Moscow: Prospekt, 2025. 271 pp. Secrets of Friendship series.

title: The Diamond Chariot
author: Boris Akunin
verdict: The channel’s author recommends this as a fictional introduction to the war and Japanese culture.
annotation: The two parts of this Fandorin novel share an intrigue. In 1905 the hero investigates preparations for sabotage on the Trans-Siberian; in 1878 he serves as vice-consul in Yokohama, meeting Masa and encountering Japanese life. The post discusses an annotated edition. The fictional plot should be distinguished from documentary history.

title: Russia and the USSR in the Wars of the Twentieth Century: Armed Forces Losses. A Statistical Study
author: Edited by G. F. Krivosheev
verdict: For studying troop numbers and losses, with care over differing categories and counting sources.
annotation: A statistical study based on archival material. The post uses it to compare Port Arthur’s garrison and armaments, army and navy losses, the defenders’ condition at surrender and prisoner numbers. It cites several divergent estimates that cannot be treated as the same measure. Moscow: OLMA-Press, 2001.
